profile.synonymsNone: An ordinal number has no synonym; it can be written as a figure with a dot (1.).

etymology.text: From Middle High German ērest, from Old High German ērist, from Proto-West Germanic *airist – originally a superlative (“earliest”).

funFacts: erste was originally the superlative of an old word for “early” – the earliest one.
pitfalls: Irregular: erste, not *einte – it does not come from eins.
Written with a dot: der 1. Mai = der erste Mai.
subtleties: Like an adjective, the ending depends on the article: der erste Tag, ein erster Tag, am ersten Tag.
erst as an adverb means “only, not until”: Ich komme erst morgen (not until tomorrow).

profile.synonymsNone: An ordinal number has no synonym; it can be written as a figure with a dot (2.).

etymology.text: From zwei + -te; it displaced the older word ander (“other, second”).

funFacts: Older German used ander (“other”) for “second”; zweite replaced it.
pitfalls: Regular: zwei + -te = zweite. Written 2.
In speech on the phone zwo is sometimes said for zwei, but the ordinal is always zweite.
subtleties: Floors are counted from the ground floor (Erdgeschoss): der erste Stock is one floor up.

etymology.text: From Old High German dritto; equivalent to drei + -te.

funFacts: Aller guten Dinge sind drei – and the third attempt (der dritte Versuch) is the lucky one.
pitfalls: Irregular: dritte, not *dreite.
zu dritt = as a group of three: Wir sind zu dritt.
subtleties: As a noun with a capital: der/die Dritte (the third person, the one in third place).

etymology.text: From Middle High German vierde, from Old High German fiordo, from Proto-West Germanic *feurþō; equivalent to vier + -te. Cognate with Dutch vierde, English fourth.

funFacts: ein Viertel (a quarter) is literally “a fourth part” (vier + Teil).
pitfalls: Do not confuse vierte (fourth) with das Viertel (a quarter): der vierte Teil = ein Viertel.
subtleties: Regular from vier: vier + -te.

pitfalls: Regular: fünf + -te = fünfte; the umlaut stays.
subtleties: In German schools, die fünfte Klasse is the first year of secondary school in most states.

subtleties: achte is also a form of the verb achten (to pay attention): ich achte darauf – a different word.

etymology.text: From Middle High German niunte, from Old High German niunto, from Proto-Germanic *newundô; equivalent to neun + -te.

funFacts: “Freude, schöner Götterfunken” from Beethoven’s Ninth is the anthem of the European Union (without words).
pitfalls: Regular: neun + -te = neunte.
subtleties: der neunte November (9 November) is a much-remembered date in German history: the fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989.

override.pos: Wiktionary files zehnte only as an ordinal numeral (“num”), while erste … neunte are filed as adjectives; it is the same kind of word (not comparable, attributive, declined like an adjective), so the course files all ordinals as ADJ (class attr). Its 36 cells were compared by hand with Wiktionary’s declension table (articles removed).

etymology.text: From Middle High German zëhente, from Old High German zehanto, from Proto-Germanic *tehundô; equivalent to zehn + -te.

funFacts: Up to 19 the ordinal adds -te (der neunzehnte), from 20 -ste (der zwanzigste, der hundertste).
pitfalls: Regular: zehn + -te; from 20 on the ending is -ste: der zwanzigste.
subtleties: der Zehnte (masculine noun) is the historical tithe, a tenth of the harvest paid to the church or lord.

etymology.text: From Middle High German lest, a contraction of leȥȥest, from Old High German leȥȥist, the superlative of laȥ (“slow, sluggish”), cognate with English late.

funFacts: English last and German letzte both go back to a superlative of late.
pitfalls: letzte Woche = last week (the one before this); die letzte Woche can also mean the final week (of the holidays). Context decides.
Declined like an adjective: der letzte, ein letzter, am letzten.
subtleties: letzt- was once a superlative of an old word for late: last is “latest”.
Never used predicatively without an ending: Er war der Letzte (he was the last one).

etymology.text: From Middle Low German helfte, derived from half (“half”); equivalent to halb + -te. The alternation -b- / -ft- also occurs in schreiben / Schrift.

funFacts: In football the usual word for a half is die Halbzeit: die erste Halbzeit, die zweite Halbzeit.
pitfalls: die Hälfte + genitive or von + dative: die Hälfte des Geldes, die Hälfte vom Geld.
With a plural noun the verb is usually singular: Die Hälfte der Schüler war krank (also waren in speech).
subtleties: Half of a thing as an adjective is halb: ein halbes Brot; the noun is die Hälfte: die Hälfte des Brotes.
meine bessere Hälfte (my better half) = my partner, said jokingly.

contrasts.value: an adverb before the next clock hour (halb acht = 7:30) or before an adjective (halb voll)

override.meaning: Wiktionary’s adverb sense is exactly this one – “a half-hour before … (used with the number of the following hour)” – written “half-hour”, which the automatic word match does not read as “half”.

profile.feeling: The clock face, thirty minutes before the hour strikes.

senses.def: half – with clock times, half an hour before the hour named (halb acht = 7:30); before an adjective: half (halb voll)

etymology.text: From Middle High German halp, from Old High German halb, from Proto-Germanic *halbaz. Compare Dutch half, English half.

funFacts: The same “half to the next hour” clock is used in Dutch (half acht) and in the Scandinavian languages.
pitfalls: halb counts towards the next hour: halb acht = 7:30, not 8:30. Think: half (on the way to) eight.
Before a noun halb is an adjective and takes endings: eine halbe Stunde (half an hour), ein halbes Jahr.
subtleties: In speech the 12-hour clock is normal: um halb acht (morning or evening); official times use 24 hours: 19:30 = neunzehn Uhr dreißig.
anderthalb / eineinhalb = one and a half; zweieinhalb = two and a half.

etymology.text: From Old High German fiorteil; equivalent to vier (“four”) + Teil (“part”).

funFacts: Fractions add -tel to the ordinal stem: Drittel, Viertel, Fünftel, Zehntel – from Teil (part).
pitfalls: das Viertel is neuter, like every fraction in -tel: das Drittel, das Fünftel.
Clock: Viertel nach acht (8:15), Viertel vor neun (8:45). In parts of the east and south: viertel neun (8:15), dreiviertel neun (8:45) – counted towards the next hour like halb.
subtleties: das Viertel is also a part of a town, a quarter or neighbourhood (das Altstadtviertel); in Austria and Bavaria ein Viertel (Wein) is a quarter litre of wine.
Fractions are built the same way: ein Drittel (a third), ein Fünftel (a fifth).

senses.def: century (a period of a hundred years)

examples.text: Das Haus ist aus dem neunzehnten Jahrhundert.

examples.text: Wir leben im einundzwanzigsten Jahrhundert.

examples.text: Die Kirche ist seit Jahrhunderten hier.
examples.tr: The church has been here for centuries.

funFacts: The 1900s are das zwanzigste Jahrhundert – like in English, the century number is one higher than the hundreds.
pitfalls: Centuries are ordinal numbers: im 19. Jahrhundert = im neunzehnten Jahrhundert (dot = ordinal).
das Jahrhundert is neuter; plural die Jahrhunderte.
subtleties: Abbreviations: Jh. or Jhdt.: im 18. Jh.
Jahrhundert- as a first part means “of the century, exceptional”: das Jahrhunderthochwasser (the flood of the century).

examples.text: Er hat zwei Jahrzehnte im Ausland gelebt.
examples.tr: He lived abroad for two decades.

examples.text: Das war das wichtigste Jahrzehnt in meinem Leben.
examples.tr: That was the most important decade of my life.

examples.text: Seit Jahrzehnten wohnen sie in diesem Dorf.
examples.tr: They have lived in this village for decades.

synonyms.nuance: decade – learned; it can also mean a period of ten days

etymology.text: An 18th-century coinage replacing the older ambiguous Dekade (“ten years; ten days”): Jahr (“year”) + zehn (“ten”) with a final -t, probably on the model of Jahrhundert, or possibly from zehnter (“tenth”).

funFacts: German needed a new word only in the 18th century: before that Dekade could mean ten years or ten days.
pitfalls: das Jahrzehnt is neuter like das Jahrhundert; plural die Jahrzehnte.
The decades of a century are named with the plural of the tens: die Achtzigerjahre / die achtziger Jahre (the eighties).
subtleties: In speech people often say die Achtziger (the 80s) instead of naming the decade.

profile.feeling: Flowers on the day you met; a nation remembering a date.

senses.def: anniversary (the same date, a number of years after an event)

examples.text: Heute ist unser Jahrestag.
examples.tr: Today is our anniversary.

examples.text: Am dritten Oktober ist der Jahrestag der deutschen Einheit.
examples.tr: The third of October is the anniversary of German unity.

examples.text: Zum zehnten Jahrestag gab es ein Fest.
examples.tr: There was a party for the tenth anniversary.

synonyms.nuance: wedding anniversary (also the wedding day itself)

etymology.text: From Middle High German jārestac, from Old High German *jāres tag; equivalent to Jahr (“year”) + -es- + Tag (“day”).

funFacts: der Tag der Deutschen Einheit (3 October) is the national holiday of Germany.
pitfalls: The joining -es- is the old genitive: Jahr-es-tag (the day of the year).
Jahrestag counts with an ordinal: der zwanzigste Jahrestag (the twentieth anniversary).
subtleties: A couple’s Jahrestag is the day they got together; the wedding anniversary is the Hochzeitstag.

senseForms.none: every meaning uses the same forms

contrasts.value: a round anniversary celebrated publicly: 25 years of a firm, a club, a job

profile.feeling: Speeches, a cake with a big number, a company photo.

senses.def: anniversary, jubilee (a round-number anniversary of an institution or of a service)

examples.text: Die Firma feiert ihr fünfzigjähriges Jubiläum.
examples.tr: The company is celebrating its fiftieth anniversary.

examples.text: Zum Jubiläum gab es ein großes Fest.
examples.tr: There was a big party for the anniversary.

examples.text: Mein Vater hatte im Mai sein Jubiläum: dreißig Jahre bei der Bahn.
examples.tr: My father had his anniversary in May: thirty years with the railway.

synonyms.nuance: the date of an event, any year – also private

etymology.text: Borrowed from Late Latin iūbilaeum, from iūbilaeus.

funFacts: The word goes back to the biblical jubilee year, which came every fifty years.
pitfalls: Plural Jubiläen (Latin -um → -en), not *Jubiläums.
A Jubiläum is counted with an adjective in -jährig: das 25-jährige (fünfundzwanzigjährige) Jubiläum.
subtleties: Jubiläum is for institutions, firms, clubs and long service; for a couple one says Jahrestag or Hochzeitstag.
